candidates.statement: For the purpose of this guidance, the term master protocol sponsor refers to the person or 70 organization who takes responsibility for and initiates the master protocol. 5 A master protocol 71 should be submitted in a new Investigational New Drug Application (IND) to FDA (see section 72 V). In many instances, individual drugs chosen for evaluation in the master protocol will also be 73 evaluated under separate INDs independent of the master protocol. A sponsor responsible for the 74 investigation of an individual drug evaluated under the separate IND is referred to as the 75 individual drug sponsor . The master protocol sponsor and the individual drug sponsor may or 76 may not be the same entity. This guidance uses the term sponsor when providing general 77 recommendations that may be relevant to both the master protocol sponsor and individual drug 78 sponsors. 79

candidates.statement: However, master protocols add elements of complexity, which can increase start-up time and 120 present design challenges (for example, in ensuring adequate blinding to treatment assignment 121 (see section III.D)). Additionally, master protocols involving multiple interested parties will 122 require a high degree of coordination. Sponsors should carefully weigh these considerations 123 when deciding whether a master protocol is appropriate as part of a drug development program. 124
candidates.context: When well-designed and well-conducted, trials using master protocols can accelerate drug 105 development by maximizing the amount of information obtained from the research effort. 106 Compared with stand-alone trials under separate protocols, a master protocol may offer logistical 107 advantages by leveraging shared protocol elements (e.g., visit schedule, measurement 108 procedures), shared infrastructure (e.g., recruitment efforts, a network of clinical sites, central 109 facilities, a central randomization system, an overarching data management system), and shared 110 oversight (e.g., by a steering committee and data monitoring committee). Some master protocols 111 may also improve efficiency by using a shared control arm in evaluating multiple drugs or by 112 leveraging information on drug effects across multiple related diseases, conditions, or disease 113 subtypes. candidates.statement: In master protocols evaluating multiple drugs with a shared control arm, sponsors should 152 consider using a randomization scheme that allocates more participants to the control arm than 153 each individual drug arm, as this can increase power for each drug-versus-control comparison for 154 a given total sample size (Chandereng et al. 2020 and Appendix: section A). Note that although 155 the randomization ratio that optimizes power involves greater-than-equal allocation to the control 156 arm, the probability that an individual participant entering the trial will be assigned to control is 157 less than in a typical two-arm controlled trial with 1:1 randomization. This disproportionate 158 randomization also reduces the risk of a poorly or highly performing control arm leading to 159 multiple correlated erroneous findings (see section III.H). 160

candidates.statement: The choice of a randomization scheme can be informed by multiple factors, including efficiency 162 and operational considerations. Randomization schemes that maintain a constant randomization 163 ratio between each drug and control can be considered. It is also possible to design a trial such 164 that the randomization ratio changes over time. This can occur when drugs enter or exit a 165 platform trial over time with certain fixed randomization schemes (i.e., schemes where the 166 randomization ratio does not depend on accumulating covariate or outcome data from the 167 platform trial). For example, one randomization scheme (see Appendix: section A) could change 168 the randomization ratio from √ 2 : 1: 1 (control:drug A:drug B) to √ 3 : 1: 1: 1 (control:drug A:drug 169 B:drug C) when a third drug, drug C, enters a trial that had been previously evaluating two drugs, 170 drug A and drug B. Another randomization scheme could maintain a constant probability of 171 being randomized to control over time, such that the randomization ratio for an individual drug 172 relative to control changes as the number of drugs evaluated in the platform trial changes. If the 173 randomization ratio for a drug relative to the control changes over time, the comparisons 174 between the drug and control should account for time periods of different randomization ratios. 175

candidates.statement: Sponsors should prespecify and justify statistical methods, including both 1) methods to evaluate 508 the primary trial objective (e.g., hypothesis tests and associated success criteria), and 2) methods 509 to estimate treatment effects with quantification of uncertainty. Statistical methods fall along a 510 continuum with respect to how information is combined or leveraged across substudies. At one 511 end of the continuum is the approach of conducting separate analyses within individual substudy 512 populations, which involves no leveraging of information across substudy populations. At the 513 other end of the continuum is the approach of conducting a single combined analysis of data 514 across the individual substudy populations and evaluating the average effect in the combined 515 populations. There are also statistical approaches that fall somewhere between the two ends of 516 the continuum and borrow some information on drug effects in other substudy populations when 517 evaluating drug effects in a given individual substudy population. These include methods (e.g., 518 Bayesian hierarchical models) in which the degree of borrowing depends on the similarity in the 519 observed effects across the substudy populations. Selecting from among the different statistical 520 approaches involves bias-variance tradeoffs. Greater borrowing of information across substudy 521 populations generally improves precision and may increase power, but also may increase bias in 522 the evaluation of drug effects in a given substudy population. 523

candidates.statement: In master protocols evaluating multiple drugs with a shared control arm, even though the 566 expected total number of type I errors is the same as in the case where the drugs are evaluated in 567 independent trials, the probability distribution for the number of type I errors 21 differs (Proschan 568 and Follmann 1995). For example, due to the correlation between hypothesis test statistics for 569 different drugs, the overall probability of committing at least one type I error is lower, whereas 570 the probability of multiple type I errors is higher, than when there are separate comparisons in 571 independent trials (e.g., Howard et al. 2018). Therefore, the probability distribution for the 572 number of type I errors (as well as other important operating characteristics, such as power) 573 should be considered both in evaluating a proposed design and analysis plan and in evaluating 574 the persuasiveness of results. For example, as noted in section III.A, use of a randomization ratio 575 other than equal allocation to have a greater proportion of participants in the control group may 576 be considered to reduce the chance of multiple correlated erroneous findings and to optimize 577 power. 578
candidates.context: In addition, it is important to control the familywise type I error probability for the evaluation of 560 each individual drug in an intended population across other sources of multiplicity (e.g., multiple 561 endpoints), just as in trials that are not conducted under a master protocol. candidates.statement: In master protocols evaluating a drug for multiple diseases, conditions, or disease subtypes in 580 different substudies, it is important to evaluate type I error probabilities and other important 581 operating characteristics, such as power, for the individual substudy populations.
